difficultyReason: The argument contains a conditional/temporal subtlety: the conclusion depends on the ink composition being fixed at the time of manufacture, not altered afterward. The necessary assumption concerns *when* the chemical signature was established, not whether the document is forged. Negation test requires careful re-reading of the inferential chain. Several distractors are topically close and sound plausible on first reading.
stimulus: Art historian: A letter purportedly written by the painter Vermeer in 1668 has been offered for sale at auction. Forensic analysts recently determined that the iron-gall ink used in the letter contains a ratio of sulfate ions to ferrous ions that matches the ratio found in ink manufactured in the Dutch Republic during the 1660s. Because no forger working after Vermeer's death could have replicated that precise ratio using materials available in later centuries, the letter must be authentic.
questionStem: The art historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron-gall inks produced in different regions of seventeenth-century Europe all shared identical sulfate-to-ferrous-ion ratios.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sulfate-to-ferrous-ion ratio in the letter's ink has not been significantly altered by chemical processes occurring after the letter was written.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vermeer personally mixed the ink he used for his correspondence rather than purchasing it from a commercial supplier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forensic analysis of ink composition is the most reliable method currently available for authenticating historical documents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No authentic letters written by Vermeer have previously been identified and sold at auction.

explanations.correct: The argument's entire evidentiary chain runs from 'the ink now has ratio R' to 'the ink was manufactured in the 1660s.' That inference holds only if the ratio measured today is the same ratio the ink had when originally applied — i.e., that post-composition chemical change has not distorted it. Negate B: the ratio *has* been significantly altered by later chemical processes. Then the current measurement no longer reflects the original ink signature, and the conclusion that the letter is authentic collapses. B is therefore necessary.
explanations.A: This is a scope-shift trap. The argument needs only that this letter's ink ratio matches 1660s Dutch Republic ink — not that all European regions shared identical ratios. Even if other regions differed, the specific match cited still supports authenticity. Negating A does not damage the argument.
explanations.C: Whether Vermeer mixed his own ink or bought it commercially is irrelevant to whether the ratio characteristic of 1660s Dutch manufacture is present. The argument depends on the ratio being a marker of period and place, not of personal production method. This is an out-of-scope distractor.
explanations.D: This is a 'too strong / sufficient' trap phrased as a comparative superlative. The argument needs only that this forensic test provides valid evidence of manufacture date — not that it is the *most reliable* method available. Negating D (i.e., some other method is more reliable) leaves the argument intact.
explanations.E: Prior auction sales of Vermeer letters have no bearing on whether this particular letter is authentic. This answer is topically continuous with the stimulus but entirely disconnected from the inferential gap the argument must bridge — a classic out-of-scope distractor.
